# Probability and stochastic processes {#sec-probability-and-stochastic-processes}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own.
:::

Epidemics in finite populations are inherently random: whether the next contact
transmits, and whether an infectious person recovers today or tomorrow, are
chance events. This unit builds the probability foundations the course needs —
random variables, the Bernoulli/Binomial family, expectation and variance, and
the idea of a discrete-time Markov chain — and applies them immediately to a
stochastic SIR model driven by binomial draws.

## Learning goals

By the end of this unit you should be able to:

- describe a Bernoulli trial and derive the Binomial distribution as a sum of
  independent trials;
- compute the mean and variance of a Binomial random variable;
- define the Markov property and explain why the binomial SIR chain has it;
- convert continuous transition rates into per-step probabilities;
- simulate an ensemble of stochastic epidemics reproducibly with `Distributions`
  and `StableRNGs`;
- compare the ensemble mean against a deterministic expectation.

## Model assumptions and classification

We model each time step of width $\delta t$ as a batch of independent Bernoulli
trials. Every susceptible individual either becomes infected or not; every
infectious individual either recovers or not. The number of new infections is
therefore Binomial in the number of susceptibles, and likewise for recoveries.
The population is closed and well mixed, and — crucially — the transition
probabilities depend only on the *current* counts $(S_t, I_t, R_t)$, not on the
history. This is the Markov property.

| Property | Classification |
|---|---|
| Determinism | Stochastic |
| Time | Discrete (step $\delta t$) |
| State | Discrete (integer counts) |
| Representation | Population (compartmental) |

## Equations

A Bernoulli$(p)$ variable takes value 1 with probability $p$. The sum of $n$
independent Bernoulli$(p)$ trials is Binomial$(n, p)$, with

$$
\Pr(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^{k}(1-p)^{n-k}, \qquad
\mathbb{E}[X] = np, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[X] = np(1-p).
$$ {#eq-p02-binomial}

Over a step of width $\delta t$, a susceptible individual is infected with
probability $p_I$ and an infectious individual recovers with probability $p_R$,
where the per-capita hazards are the SIR rates converted through
@eq-p01-rate:

$$
p_I = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{\beta c I_t}{N}\,\delta t\right), \qquad
p_R = 1 - \exp\!\left(-\gamma\,\delta t\right).
$$ {#eq-p02-probs}

The chain then updates by drawing the two event counts and moving individuals
between compartments:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_t &\sim \text{Binomial}(S_t, p_I), &\quad Z_t &\sim \text{Binomial}(I_t, p_R),\\
S_{t+1} &= S_t - Y_t, &\quad
I_{t+1} &= I_t + Y_t - Z_t, &\quad
R_{t+1} &= R_t + Z_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-p02-chain}

Because every individual moves *forward* through S→I→R and none are created or
destroyed, $S_{t+1}+I_{t+1}+R_{t+1} = S_t+I_t+R_t = N$ for all $t$.

## Julia implementation

The kernel below maps @eq-p02-probs and @eq-p02-chain directly onto code. The
random number generator `rng` is passed explicitly so that the stochastic stream
is reproducible and local. `Binomial(n, p)` from `Distributions` is exactly the
distribution in @eq-p02-binomial.

```{julia}
#| label: p02-kernel
using Distributions, StableRNGs

rate_to_proportion(r, δt) = -expm1(-r * δt)

function sir_markov_step(state, p, δt, rng)
    S, I, R = state
    β, c, γ, N = p
    p_I = rate_to_proportion(β * c * I / N, δt)   # eq-p02-probs
    p_R = rate_to_proportion(γ, δt)
    Y = rand(rng, Binomial(S, p_I))               # new infections
    Z = rand(rng, Binomial(I, p_R))               # new recoveries
    return (S - Y, I + Y - Z, R + Z)              # eq-p02-chain
end

function simulate_chain(u0, p, δt, nsteps, rng)
    traj = Matrix{Int}(undef, 3, nsteps + 1)
    traj[:, 1] .= u0
    state = Tuple(u0)
    for k in 1:nsteps
        state = sir_markov_step(state, p, δt, rng)
        traj[:, k + 1] .= state
    end
    return traj
end
```

We run an ensemble of 200 realisations from the baseline initial condition and
also record the ensemble mean of the infectious compartment.

```{julia}
#| label: p02-ensemble
u0 = [990, 10, 0]                 # integer S, I, R
p  = (0.05, 10.0, 0.25, 1000)     # β, c, γ, N
δt = 1.0
nsteps = 40
nsims = 200

ensemble = [simulate_chain(u0, p, δt, nsteps, StableRNG(seed))
            for seed in 1:nsims]
I_paths = reduce(hcat, (traj[2, :] for traj in ensemble))  # (nsteps+1) × nsims
mean_I = vec(sum(I_paths; dims = 2)) ./ nsims
(size(I_paths), round(maximum(mean_I); digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-p02-ensemble
#| fig-cap: "Two hundred stochastic SIR realisations of the infectious compartment (thin grey) with the ensemble mean overlaid (red). Individual epidemics fluctuate and some fade early, but the mean traces a smooth, reproducible curve."
using CairoMakie

ts = 0:nsteps
fig = Figure(size = (680, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "infectious I(t)",
          title = "Binomial SIR chain: 200 realisations")
for j in 1:nsims
    lines!(ax, ts, I_paths[:, j]; color = (:grey, 0.15), linewidth = 1)
end
lines!(ax, ts, mean_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "ensemble mean")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

## Validation

For a single Binomial draw the sample mean over many replicates must approach
the theoretical mean $np$ from @eq-p02-binomial. We check this directly:

```{julia}
#| label: p02-check-binomial
rng = StableRNG(7)
n, prob = 990, 0.02
samples = [rand(rng, Binomial(n, prob)) for _ in 1:100_000]
theoretical = n * prob
empirical = sum(samples) / length(samples)
(theoretical, round(empirical; digits = 3), isapprox(empirical, theoretical; rtol = 0.02))
```

As a structural check on the chain itself, every realisation must conserve the
population exactly (@eq-p02-chain moves integers between compartments):

```{julia}
#| label: p02-check-conservation
totals = [sum(traj[:, k]) for traj in ensemble for k in 1:nsteps+1]
all(==(1000), totals)
```

Both checks pass: the empirical Binomial mean matches $np$ to within 2%, and all
$200 \times 41$ population totals equal $N = 1000$.

## Interpretation and limitations

The binomial chain captures *demographic stochasticity* — the randomness of a
finite population — that the deterministic ODE ignores. Individual epidemics can
peak at different times or fade out entirely, yet the ensemble mean tracks a
smooth trajectory close to the deterministic solution we study in
@sec-foundations. The binomial construction, however, allows more than one event
per individual per step to be double-counted only if $p_I + p_R$ per compartment
were mishandled; here susceptibles and infectious individuals are treated in
separate binomials, which is exact only in the limit of small $\delta t$. It
also assumes infections and recoveries within a step are independent. The
exact, event-by-event alternative — the Gillespie algorithm of @gillespie1977 —
is developed in the continuous-time Markov chapter. For the distributions API
see the [Distributions.jl documentation](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/).

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#p02-ex1}

The variance of a Binomial$(n,p)$ is $np(1-p)$ (@eq-p02-binomial). Draw
100 000 samples from `Binomial(990, 0.02)` using `StableRNG(7)` and compare the
sample variance with the theoretical value. Then repeat with $p = 0.5$ and
explain, using the formula, why the variance is largest near $p = 0.5$.

### Exercise 2 {#p02-ex2}

Reduce the step width to $\delta t = 0.1$ (and increase `nsteps` to 400 so the
horizon is unchanged) and rerun the ensemble. Report how the fraction of
realisations that reach $I = 0$ before day 40 changes, and explain why finer
steps change the discrete-time dynamics.
